gloss_terse: A song or psalm of praise; a musical composition celebrating God or expressing triumph.
gloss_readable: Derived from the root zamar ('to sing, make music'), this noun denotes a song or psalm — especially one of praise or worship. David is famously called the 'sweet singer of Israel's songs' (2 Sam 23:1), and the Psalms employ it for joyful worship (Ps 95:2, 119:54). In Isaiah it can also refer to a hostile song of triumph (Isa 25:5), showing the word covers the full range of composed vocal music, from devotional hymn to victory chant.

senses.1: A song, psalm, or musical composition — particularly one of praise or worship. The English 'songs' and Spanish 'canticos' consistently point to vocal compositions. Used of David's psalms (2 Sam 23:1), nighttime songs from God (Job 35:10), shouts of worship (Ps 95:2), statutes treasured as songs (Ps 119:54), and even the triumphant song of ruthless oppressors (Isa 25:5). The French 'chant' likewise captures the idea of a sung piece rather than mere speech.

gloss_terse: Fierce rage, stormy fury, or violent indignation — of kings, of God, or of the raging sea.
gloss_readable: A poetic and late noun conveying fierce, stormy rage. It describes the violent anger of King Asa, who imprisoned the seer Hanani 'in a rage' (2 Chr 16:10), and the fury of God's judgment (Isa 30:30, Mic 7:9). Proverbs compares a king's wrath to a lion's roar (Prov 19:12). Strikingly, Jonah 1:15 applies it to the raging of the sea, connecting human fury with nature's untamed violence.

senses.1: Rage, fury, or stormy indignation — whether of a human ruler, of God, or of natural forces. Spanish 'ira' and 'furor,' alongside French 'colere,' confirm the core meaning of fierce anger. Applied to King Asa's violent outrage (2 Chr 16:10), divine wrath (Isa 30:30 'raging of anger'), a king's roaring fury (Prov 19:12), and the storm-tossed sea subsiding once Jonah is cast overboard (Jonah 1:15). The word bridges personal wrath and cosmic tempest.

gloss_terse: Old age; the advanced stage of life, often paired with grey hair as a marker of long years.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun meaning 'old age,' frequently paired with 'grey hair' (sevah) to evoke the fullness of a long life. It appears in poignant pleas not to be abandoned in old age (Ps 71:9, 18), in the account of Sarah bearing Isaac after her old age (Gen 24:36), and in noting Solomon's spiritual decline 'at the time of his old age' (1 Kgs 11:4). The word marks a recognized life-stage carrying both honor and vulnerability.

senses.1: The state or period of old age — advanced years in a person's life. Spanish 'vejez' and French 'ancien-age' uniformly render the concept. The psalmist pleads not to be cast off in old age (Ps 71:9) and asks God to sustain him unto grey hair (Ps 71:18). It frames Sarah's miraculous childbearing (Gen 24:36), Solomon's decline into idolatry (1 Kgs 11:4), and Asa's foot disease (1 Kgs 15:23). Paired with sevah ('grey hair'), it represents the culmination of a life's journey.

gloss_terse: Zerahite — a member of the clan descended from Zerah, son of Judah (or Simeon).
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective always used with the definite article, designating a member of the clan of Zerah. In most occurrences it refers to descendants of Zerah son of Judah (Num 26:20; Josh 7:17; 1 Chr 27:11, 13), while one instance traces to Zerah son of Simeon (Num 26:13). The famous episode of Achan's sin identifies him through this clan marker (Josh 7:17), and David's military commanders include Zerahites in the monthly rotation.

senses.1: A gentilic designation for descendants of Zerah — primarily the Judahite clan (Num 26:20, Josh 7:17, 1 Chr 27:11, 13), and also the Simeonite branch (Num 26:13). English renders it 'Zerahite,' Spanish 'zerahita/zerajitas,' and French 'Zerahite/Zarchite.' Always appears with the article (hazzarchi) as a collective noun. The Achan narrative (Josh 7:17) narrows down from tribe to clan to household using this designation, and Davidic military rosters list Zerahite officers.

gloss_terse: Hebronite — a member of the Levitical clan descended from Hebron son of Kohath.
gloss_readable: A gentilic adjective identifying members of the Levitical family descended from Hebron, a son of Kohath. Always used with the article as a collective noun, it appears exclusively in administrative and cultic contexts: the census of Levitical families (Num 3:27; 26:58) and David's organization of temple duties (1 Chr 26:23, 30, 31). The Hebronites were assigned responsibilities both within the sanctuary and in civil administration west and east of the Jordan.

senses.1: A gentilic adjective for the Levitical clan descended from Hebron son of Kohath. English 'Hebronite,' Spanish 'hebronita,' and French 'Hebronite' all reflect the clan designation. Appears in the Levitical census lists (Num 3:27; 26:58) and in David's administrative organization where Hebronites served as overseers for religious and civil matters on both sides of the Jordan (1 Chr 26:23, 30, 31). Always with the article as a collective noun identifying the family group.

gloss_terse: To declare, tell, make known — a poetic Aramaic-influenced verb used for announcing wisdom or truth.
gloss_readable: A verb found only in the Piel stem in poetic and late texts, meaning 'to declare' or 'make known.' As an Aramaic loanword (cognate with chavvei), it carries a formal, deliberate quality of announcement. Elihu uses it repeatedly in Job to introduce his declarations of wisdom (Job 15:17; 32:6, 10, 17; 36:2). The Psalms employ it for the heavens declaring knowledge night after night (Ps 19:3), giving the word a cosmic scope alongside its human forensic usage.

senses.1: To tell, declare, or make known — used in formal, deliberate speech acts. Spanish 'declarare' and French 'annoncer' both capture the proclamatory tone. Elihu is the primary user, solemnly declaring his opinion and knowledge (Job 32:6, 10, 17; 36:2), while Eliphaz also employs it (Job 15:17). In Psalm 19:3, the night sky itself 'declares knowledge' to successive nights. The Aramaic coloring suits the elevated, quasi-judicial register of these wisdom and hymnic contexts.

gloss_terse: Writhing pain, anguish, or birth-pangs — severe physical or emotional distress likened to labor.
gloss_readable: A noun denoting sharp, convulsive pain — whether the physical contortions of fear or the anguish of labor. Its most vivid usage compares military or national dread to the pangs of a woman in childbirth (Ps 48:6; Mic 4:9; Jer 6:24; 50:43). In Exodus 15:14, it describes the writhing terror that seized the nations at news of Israel's deliverance. The birth-pang metaphor recurs so consistently that the word almost always evokes labor imagery.

senses.1: Writhing pain, anguish, or birth-pangs — intense physical or emotional distress. Spanish 'dolor' and French 'angoisse' both capture the core sense of acute suffering. At the Exodus, peoples writhed in fear (Exod 15:14). Allied kings attacking Jerusalem seized up 'like a woman in labor' (Ps 48:6). Zion writhes before Assyria (Mic 4:9), and Judah and Babylon alike suffer anguish compared to childbirth (Jer 6:24; 22:23; 50:43). The simile 'like a woman giving birth' is almost formulaic with this noun.

gloss_terse: A flute or reed pipe — a wind instrument used in both celebration and mourning.
gloss_readable: A masculine noun for a wind instrument, likely a reed flute or pipe. It appears in festive contexts — the people playing flutes at Solomon's coronation so loudly the earth shook (1 Kgs 1:40) — and in lists of instruments at feasts (Isa 5:12). Isaiah 30:29 pairs it with joyful night processions to God's mountain. Yet Jeremiah 48:36 uses its sound as a simile for mourning over Moab, showing the flute served both celebration and lament in ancient Israel.

senses.1: A flute or reed pipe — a wind instrument for both joyful and sorrowful occasions. Spanish 'flauta(s)' and English 'flutes' confirm the consistent identification as a wind instrument. Used in Samuel's description of prophetic bands (1 Sam 10:5), Solomon's coronation festivities (1 Kgs 1:40), Isaiah's critique of banquets (Isa 5:12), and a joyful pilgrimage procession (Isa 30:29). Jeremiah 48:36 turns it to lament, where the flute's wail sounds for Moab's destruction — demonstrating the instrument's dual emotional register.

gloss_terse: Desire, delight, preciousness — that which is attractive, pleasant, or coveted.
gloss_readable: A masculine noun expressing what is desirable or delightful. Always appearing after a construct noun, it functions as an intensifying attribute: 'vineyards of delight' (Amos 5:11), 'fields of delight' (Isa 32:12), and 'young men of desire' — that is, attractive, desirable young men (Ezek 23:6, 12, 23). Spanish 'deleite' and 'delicia' capture the aesthetic pleasure, while 'deseo' emphasizes the longing quality. The word elevates the ordinary into the coveted.

senses.1: That which is desirable, delightful, or precious — used attributively to mark something as especially attractive or coveted. Spanish 'deleite/delicia/deseo' captures both the pleasure and longing dimensions. Amos speaks of 'vineyards of delight' that the unjust planted (Amos 5:11), Isaiah mourns 'pleasant fields' (Isa 32:12), and Ezekiel describes Assyrian officers as 'desirable young men' to portray Oholibah's infatuation (Ezek 23:6, 12, 23). The word consistently elevates its head noun into something especially prized.

gloss_terse: Vinegar or sour wine — a sharp acidic liquid used as a condiment, drink, and in proverbial similes.
gloss_readable: A masculine noun for vinegar or sour wine, a common condiment in the ancient Near East. Ruth dipped her bread in vinegar at Boaz's table (Ruth 2:14), while the Nazirite vow specifically prohibited both wine-vinegar and beer-vinegar (Num 6:3). Proverbs employs it memorably in similes: vinegar on the teeth for the sluggard's irritating effect (Prov 10:26), and vinegar on soda for the futility of singing songs to a heavy heart (Prov 25:20). The psalmist received it in place of water as an act of cruelty (Ps 69:21).

senses.1: Vinegar or sour wine — a sharp, fermented liquid. Spanish 'vinagre' and French 'vinaigre' render it uniformly. Served as an everyday condiment for dipping bread (Ruth 2:14) but forbidden to Nazirites in both wine and beer varieties (Num 6:3). Used figuratively for harshness: given to the thirsty psalmist as mockery (Ps 69:21), compared to the irritation a sluggard causes (Prov 10:26 'like vinegar to the teeth'), and paired with natron to illustrate the discord of merry songs sung to a grieving heart (Prov 25:20).
